newsitem.title: GUYANA: FOCUS - Guyana's economic recovery on target.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Guyana's economic recovery on target.

text.p: Guyana's economy, firmly on the road to recovery, is likely to grow by more than seven percent this year, maintaining the high average growth rate of the past four years, Finance Minister Bharrat Jagdeo said.
"This year we targeted real (gross domestic product) GDP growth of 6.6 percent, but we think it will exceed seven percent," he told Reuters in an interview.

Still one of Latin America's poorest nations, the former British colony has enjoyed a relative economic boom in recent years following two decades of state control and socialist experiments that had sent it on a steady downhill slide.
But Jagdeo said the shift towards a market-oriented economy would probably be a long haul in a thinly-populated, agricultural country lacking proper infrastructure and managerial skills.
"We need to keep that GDP growth for the next 15 years to really transform the economy," he said.
Inflation, from a high 105 percent in 1989, fell to 16.1 percent in 1995.
"It will be around 7.5 percent this year," Jagdeo said.

With a population of 800,000 -- and as many living outside the country, mostly in the United States, Canada and Britain -- Guyana has implemented major economic reforms in recent years under programs supported by the International Monetary Fund.

In May, Guyana, which until recently was saddled with the heaviest debt burden in the world at $2.1 billion, won a major agreement from the Paris Club of creditor nations. It was awarded the "Naples Terms", a far-reaching debt relief deal consisting of a 67 percent stock of debt reduction with Paris Club creditors and the neighbouring island state of Trinidad and Tobago.

Calling Guyana's economy "the freest in the Caribbean...with no sector barred from foreign capital," Jagdeo said the administration of President Cheddi Jagan would continue to cut the bloated public sector and try to woo foreign investors.

He said an "aggressive privatization program" this year focused on six entities with a combined value of $84 million, apart from the key Guyana Electricity Corp (GEC) and Linmine, a bauxite producing company.

The six are: Guyana Co-operative Insurance Service, Guyana Stock Feeds, Guyana National Printers, the National Edible Oil Company (NEOCOL), Guyana Stores and the National Bank of Industry and Commerce (NBIC).

Foreign diplomats and economic experts said the privatization of GEC was paramount in a country that has been plagued by a deficient supply of electric power for years. Blackouts are still a daily occurrence in Georgetown.
The state intends to retain 40 percent of GEC with another 40 percent offered to foreign investors. The remaining 20 percent would go to the local private sector through an IPO.

Partners are due to be selected in January and an agreement could be reached by March 1997, government sources said. GEC, which practically collapsed last year, needs up to $150 million in the next 10 years to operate properly, the sources said.
GEC privatization would be "a tremendously symbolic measure," Charles Greenwood, the Inter-American Development Bank (IDB) representative in Guyana, said.
"Perception still exists of Guyana being distrustful of foreigners but if GEC is privatized that will be a strong clue," he told Reuters.

Greenwood said Guyana, with vast resources in agriculture, forestry and mining, had no other option than opening up to foreign capital "because traditional aid pots of money (from the IDB, the World Bank, etc) are declining worldwide."
"The key to the future of Guyana is private investment."
President Jagan agreed. But he stressed in a separate interview that he intended to do it without jeopardizing what he called "social gains for the working people".
Jagan, a 78-year-old onetime Marxist, became president in October 1992 after his People's Progressive Party won the country's first democratic elections in 28 years.
"Regarding foreign investment, we're trying to do our best and we're trying to do it faster" he said, but fundamental weaknesses in the public sector hamper global economic growth.

"There is administrative incapacity," he admitted, saying it would take years to offset consequences of the brain drain of the 1980s. A foreign businessman summed it up harshly: "If you find a competent minister, you're lucky."
Despite these shortcomings including the lack of an investor's code, Guyana has carried out "one of the most successful (IMF) adjustment program anywhere," Greenwood said.
"People know Jagan's heart was not in it," he added but the president himself acknowledged: "We had no alternative."
-- Caracas newsroom, 582 505 2600
